paper_metadata.title: Association Between Socioeconomic Deprivation and Functional Impairment After Stroke: The South London Stroke Register

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a well-established, prospective population-based register (SLSR) with clear geographic and diagnostic criteria. While there is a loss of patients before the 3-month assessment, the source population and baseline characteristics are thoroughly described.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: recording all first-ever strokes in patients of all ages living in 22 electoral wards in Lambeth and Southwark (total population at the 2011 census were 357308) in South London.
items.reasoning: The target population is clearly defined by geography, age, and clinical event (first-ever stroke).

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: The SLSR methodology has been fully described before.10,11 In brief, the SLSR is an ongoing prospective populationbased stroke register
items.reasoning: The use of a validated, ongoing population-based register minimizes recruitment bias compared to hospital-only samples.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Data collected between January 1995 and December 2011 were used in this analysis.
items.reasoning: The start and end dates for the study period are explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: living in 22 electoral wards in Lambeth and Southwark... in South London.
items.reasoning: The specific geographic location and administrative wards are provided.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: recording all first-ever strokes in patients of all ages... The diagnosis of stroke, using the World Health Organization clinical definition, was verified by a study clinician
items.reasoning: The study uses the WHO clinical definition and specifies 'first-ever stroke' as the primary inclusion criterion.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: 4414 people with first-ever stroke were registered, of whom 1171 (26.5%) died before 3 months, 2128 (48.2%) had a 3-month assessment, and 1115 (25.3%) were lost to follow up
items.reasoning: While the register aims for all cases, the 25.3% lost to follow-up (excluding deaths) is significant, and it is unclear if these individuals differ from participants.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Data of hypertension... myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, peripheral vascular disease, previous transient ischemic attack, diabetes mellitus, and current smoking status were collected.
items.reasoning: Extensive baseline clinical and sociodemographic data were collected and reported.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: There is a high rate of loss to follow-up (25.3% at 3 months). While the authors mention these patients 'declined, not traced in time, or moved away', there is limited analysis comparing the characteristics of those lost to follow-up versus those who completed the study, which could introduce attrition bias.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 2128 (48.2%) had a 3-month assessment, and 1115 (25.3%) were lost to follow up (declined, not traced in time, or moved away).
items.reasoning: Less than 50% of the total registered sample was available for the 3-month functional assessment, though a large portion of the 'missing' were due to mortality (26.5%).

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text describes the reasons for loss but does not detail specific attempts to retrieve data for those who declined or were not traced.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: declined, not traced in time, or moved away
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly list the reasons for attrition.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide a table or comparison of baseline characteristics for the 1115 patients lost to follow-up.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without a comparison of the 'lost to follow-up' group, it is impossible to determine if the analyzed sample is biased.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (SED) is measured using a validated, objective national index (IMD 2007) based on postcodes. This method is standardized and independent of the outcome measurement.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: socioeconomic deprivation was measured using the index of multiple deprivation based on patient postcodes
items.reasoning: The IMD is a well-defined composite measure described in detail in the methods.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: IMD is a composite measure of relative deprivation at a small-area level... The 32 482 lower super output areas in England were ranked
items.reasoning: The IMD is a standard UK government metric, ensuring high reliability and validity.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: we divided patients into 4 groups according to the quartiles of the IMD score.
items.reasoning: Quartiles are a standard way to handle IMD scores to avoid data-dredging for optimal cut-points.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: we calculated the index of multiple deprivation (IMD) 200712 to measure the baseline SED for each patient.
items.reasoning: The same postcode-based calculation was applied to all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: 2109 had BI measured, of whom 2104 had IMD scores for analysis.
items.reasoning: Only 5 patients were missing the PF data among those with the outcome measured.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Missing data for PF was minimal (5 cases), so they were likely excluded; no imputation was mentioned.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (functional impairment) was measured using the Barthel Index, a gold-standard tool in stroke research. Assessments were performed by trained interviewers at fixed time points.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: functional impairment after stroke was defined as a Barthel index of <15.
items.reasoning: The outcome is clearly defined using a validated scale and a specific threshold.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: All follow-up assessments included in this study were completed by December 31, 2011... All interviewers underwent regular standardized training in the use of the different scales.
items.reasoning: The Barthel Index is a validated tool, and the use of trained interviewers enhances reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Follow-up data were collected by validated postal codes or face-to-face interviews with patients or their carers.
items.reasoning: Standardized follow-up protocols were applied to the entire cohort.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study performed extensive multivariable adjustment for a wide range of clinical and demographic confounders, including prestroke disability and stroke severity, which are critical in prognosis studies.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, living conditions before stroke, years of stroke occurring, admitted to hospital, smoking habits, hypertension, prestroke BI <15, prestroke comorbidities... stroke subtype, Glasgow coma scale, speech deficit, and acute care
items.reasoning: The list of measured confounders is comprehensive, covering demographics, comorbidities, and acute care.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: hypertension (general practice or hospital records of high blood pressure >140 mmHg systolic or >90 mmHg diastolic)... Glasgow Coma Scale, dichotomized to <13 (severe/ moderate) and ≥13 (mild)
items.reasoning: Clinical confounders are defined with specific thresholds or scales.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The diagnosis of stroke... was verified by a study clinician... clinical details at the time of maximal impairment.
items.reasoning: Confounders were measured through clinical examination and verified records.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The SLSR methodology has been fully described before... recording all first-ever strokes
items.reasoning: Standardized register protocols ensure consistent measurement across the cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not mention imputation for missing confounder data; it appears complete-case analysis was used.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: We further analyzed data stratified by age, sex, prestroke comorbidities, and stroke subtype.
items.reasoning: The study used stratification to explore the impact of key variables.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: We used multivariate-adjusted logistic regression models to compute odds ratios
items.reasoning: Logistic regression was used to adjust for a comprehensive set of potential confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are appropriate for the study design. The authors report both short-term (3 months) and long-term (3 years) results, and the use of logistic regression with pre-specified confounders is sound.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: We used multivariate-adjusted logistic regression models... All analyses were performed using Stata, version 13
items.reasoning: The analytical approach is clearly described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: In the logistic models, we adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, living conditions... stroke subtype, Glasgow coma scale, speech deficit, and acute care
items.reasoning: The model includes variables known to influence stroke outcome (severity, age, care).

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: multivariate-adjusted logistic regression models to compute odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals
items.reasoning: Logistic regression is appropriate for the binary outcome (BI <15 vs >=15).

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 shows the number and adjusted odds ratio... Table 2... Table 3... Table 4... Table 5
items.reasoning: The study reports results for the primary association and all stratified analyses mentioned in the methods.
